L93: ABSTRACT
L94: 
L95: Anthropogenic sources, especially industrial, emit into the at-
L96: 
L97: mosphere gases and aerosols, which play an important role
L98: 
L99: in atmospheric exchanges. The use of new hyperspectral air-
L100: 
L101: borne sensors in the infrared range at high spatial resolution
L102: opens the way for further improvements in the characteriza-
L103: 
L104: tion of industrial plumes. Existing methods, based on linear
L105: 
L106: or Bayesian approach, present two major limitations: the het-
L107: 
L108: erogeneous environment impact on retrievals and the spatial
L109: 
L110: and vertical extents of the plume are not considered.
L111: 
L112: In this paper, a new method for plume characterization is pre-
L113: 
L114: sented to overcome such limitations. This method uses an
L115: 
L116: accurate non linear formalism of cloud gas radiative impact.
L117: It includes furthermore a ground classiﬁcation of the scene,
L118: 
L119: in order to take into account the soil heterogeneity and spec-
L120: 
L121: tral behaviour. This strategy will be validated using synthetic
L122: 
L123: scenes of industrial area, and real data from Telops Hyper-
L124: 
L125: Cam airborne platform.
L126: 
L127: Index Terms—hyperspectral, plume, gas, thermal in-
L128: 
L129: frared, detection, characterization, Levenberg-Marquardt.

L131: 1. INTRODUCTION
L132: 
L133: Anthropogenic sources, especially industrial, are involved
L134: with a major contribution to air pollution. However, these
L135: 
L136: emissions remain poorly estimated at a high spatial resolu-
L137: 
L138: tion. Recent technological advances in terms of spatial and
L139: 
L140: spectral resolutions of thermal infrared airborne hyperspectral
L141: 
L142: sensors, open a way of improving gaseous efﬂuents charac-
L143: 
L144: terization, since the majority of gas have their signatures in
L145: 
L146: the thermal domain.
L147: 
L148: In literature different approaches were proposed to quan-
L149: 
L150: tify gaseous efﬂuents using hyperspectral infrared imagery.
L151: Assuming plume gases are optically thin, Young [1] intro-
L152: 
L153: duces a linear formalism to retrieve plume integrated column
L154: 
L155: concentration of each pixel. A linear least-squares regression
L156: 
L157: method is used to determine the thermal contrast, which is di-
L158: 
L159: rectly related to the integrated column concentration.
L160: 
L161: Heasler, et al. [2] follow a Bayesian approach. They devel-
L162: 
L163: oped a non-linear regression using the Metropolis-Hastings
L164: 
L165: algorithm. The atmospheric terms are supposed to be known.
L166: As the background clutter (ground temperature and emissiv-
L167: 
L168: ity) is the dominant source of variability, it is handled as nui-
L169: 
L170: sance parameters.
L171: 
L172: A previous study [3] showed some of the limitations of
L173: 
L174: such characterization methods. First, the spatial and vertical
L175: 
L176: extents of the plume are not taken into account in these meth-
L177: 
L178: ods, which induces a miscalculation of the plume radiative
L179: 
L180: impact. Then, the heterogeneous environment of an indus-
L181: trial scene impact a lot on the retrieval performances of these
L182: 
L183: methods [4].
L184: 
L185: Hereinafter, we present a new method of plume characteriza-
L186: 
L187: tion, which takes into account the vertical extent of the plume.
L188: 
L189: Moreover, our retrieval is preceded by a classiﬁcation of the
L190: 
L191: background, in order to deal with soil heterogeneity.
L192: 
L193: The paper is organized in the following way: section 2 is ded-
L194: 
L195: icated to the description of the plume retrieval methodology.
L196: Then, sections 3 and 4 evaluate the application of our method
L197: 
L198: on synthetic data and Telops Hyper-Cam airborne platform
L199: 
L200: data.

The use of the new hyperspectral airborne image sensors in the thermal infrared range opens the way to new development to improve plume remote sensing.
L673: The thermal domain (MWIR-LWIR) spectrometry has been employed for decades to detect and estimate gaseous pollutants. Indeed, the majority of gas plume have their signature in the thermal domain. However, the impact of plume’s temperature and the heterogeneity of ground properties make the gas characterization more difficult. Existing methods have several limitations: (i) the heterogeneous environment impact on their performances; (ii) spatial and vertical extent of the plume is not taken into account.
L674: In this work, a new method for characterizing gas plumes is presented to overcome such limitations. This method is based on an accurate non linear formalism of cloud gas radiative impact. It includes: (i) a ground classification of the scene, in order to take account the soil's heterogeneity and spectral behavior; (ii) and an optimal estimation formalism taking into account constraint on spatial and vertical plume structure.

Heasler L690:   * cite26†Christian Posse L691:   * cite27†Jeffrey Hylden L692:   * cite28†Kevin Anderson L693: This paper presents a nonlinear Bayesian regression algorithm for detecting and estimating gas plume content from hyper-spectral data. Remote sensing data, by its very nature, is collected under less controlled conditions than laboratory data. As a result, the physics-based model that is used to describe the relationship between the observed remote-sensing spectra, and the terrestrial (or atmospheric) parameters that are estimated is typically littered with many unknown “nuisance” parameters.
L694: Bayesian methods are well-suited for this context as they automatically incorporate the uncertainties associated with all nuisance parameters into the error estimates of the parameters of interest. The nonlinear Bayesian regression methodology is illustrated on simulated data from a three-layer model for longwave infrared (LWIR) measurements from a passive instrument.
L695: The generated LWIR scenes contain plumes of varying intensities, and this allows estimation uncertainty and probability of detection to be quantified. The results show that this approach should permit more accurate estimation as well as a more reasonable description of estimate uncertainty. Specifically, the methodology produces a standard error that is more realistic than that produced by matched filter estimation.

This study uses a modified k-means clustering to improve matched filter performance. Several simple bivariate cases are examined in detail, and the interaction of filtering and partitioning is discussed. The authors show that clustering can reduce within-class variance and group pixels with similar correlation structures. Both of these features improve filter performance.
L713: The traditional k-means algorithm is modified to work with a sample of the image at each iteration and is tested against two hyperspectral datasets. A new “extreme” centroid initialization technique is introduced and shown to speed convergence. Several matched filtering formulations (the simple matched filter, the clutter matched filter, and the saturated matched filter) are compared for a variety of number of classes and synthetic hyperspectral images.
L714: The performance of the various clutter matched filter formulations is similar, all are about an order of magnitude better than the simple matched filter. Clustering is found to improve the performance of all matched filter formulations by a factor of two to five. Clustering in conjunction with clutter matched filtering can improve fifty-fold over the simple case, enabling very weak signals to be detected in hyperspectral images
